This page is executable:
every code block below is run when the documentation is built,
and the output shown is the real output.

## Imports

The top-level `openmusickit` namespace holds what any piece of music is built from,
whatever its musical system:
the graph, the objects placed in it,
and the values that belong to no one system.
A musical system is opted into separately.
Western Standard Music Notation (WSMN) has its types in `wsmn`
and its ready-made vocabulary
(pitches, intervals, chord types, durations, time signatures, marks, clefs)
in `wsmn.symbols`.

```{python}
import openmusickit as omk
from openmusickit.systems import wsmn
from openmusickit.systems.wsmn.symbols import *
```

## Tones

In WSMN,
a tone is a `TonalVector`:
a tuple of (diatonic letter index, chromatic pitch class, octave).
Middle C is octave 0 internally,
but strings and display default to the usual middle C = C4 convention.

```{python}
c4 = wsmn.TonalVector.from_string("C4")
fs5 = wsmn.TonalVector.from_string("F#5")
bb3 = wsmn.TonalVector.from_string("Bb3")

print(repr(c4))
print(repr(fs5))
print(f"{c4}  {fs5}  {bb3}")
print(f"{fs5:ascii}")
```

Pitch-class symbols with no octave are ready-made in `wsmn.symbols`.
An `x` is a sharp and a `b` is a flat.

```{python}
print(f"{C}  {Cx}  {Eb}  {G}")
print(f"{C.qualify_octave(0)}")
```

## Intervals and transposition

A `TonalVector` is also an interval,
and the same class represents both.
Transpose a tone by adding an interval to it,
or by calling `transpose` with a direction.

```{python}
print(f"{c4 + M3}")
print(f"{c4 + P5}")
print(f"{c4.transpose(M3, wsmn.TonalDirection.DOWN)}")
print(f"{c4 - m7}")
```

The interval between two tones is their `distance`.

```{python}
e4 = c4 + M3
gap = c4.distance(e4)
print(gap.interval.unicode, "=", abs(gap), "half steps")
```

## Durations

A `MetricalDuration` is a fraction of a whole note, with optional dots.
`wsmn.symbols` provides the common ones by name.

```{python}
print(repr(wsmn.MetricalDuration(1, 4)))
print(repr(wsmn.MetricalDuration(3, 4)))
print(dotted_half.rational_length)
print(repr(quarter + eighth))
```

## Notes and rests

A `NoteEvent` holds a set of tones (one for a single note, several for a chord in one voice)
and a duration.
A `Rest` is a `NoteEvent` holding a silent tone.

```{python}
note = omk.NoteEvent(tones={c4}, duration=quarter)
rest = omk.Rest(quarter)

print(note)
print(rest)
print(rest.is_rest)
```

Transposing a note transforms its tones in place.

```{python}
note.transform_tones(wsmn.TonalVector.transpose, P5)
print(f"{next(iter(note.tones))}")
```

## Chords and keys

A chord is a chord type realized at a root.
Calling a root with a chord type, or a chord type with a root, does the same thing.

```{python}
print(C(maj), G(dom7), D(min_))
print(C(maj) / E)
print([f"{t}" for t in C(maj)])
```

A key is a tonic and a mode.

```{python}
d_major = wsmn.Key.of(D, Major)
print(d_major.name)
print(d_major.signature)
print([f"{t}" for t in d_major.tones])
```

## Lyrics

`parse_lyrics` splits text into syllables.
Hyphens split a word into syllables and whitespace separates words.

```{python}
for syllable in omk.parse_lyrics("Twin-kle, twin-kle, lit-tle star"):
    print(f"{str(syllable):10}  {syllable.placement.value:8}  {syllable.word}")
```

## A small score graph

Musical objects become nodes in an `OmkGraph`.
A *line* is a chain of events joined by NEXT edges.
Independent lines are related in time by pinning one event to another
with a SIMULTANEOUS edge.
Lyrics are a line of syllables,
each attached to the note where it begins with a LYRIC edge.
A `Score` carries the work's metadata and names the component:
it points at the heads of its lines.
A clef, like a key or a meter, is a zero-duration `ClefEvent`
at the point in the line where it takes effect.

Here is the first phrase of *Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star*:
a melody under a treble clef, its lyrics, and a chord line above it.

```{python}
graph = omk.OmkGraph(omk.GraphMeta())
score = omk.Score(title="Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star", lyricist="Jane Taylor")

# The melody: a clef, then one line of NoteEvents.
pitches = "C4 C4 G4 G4 A4 A4 G4  F4 F4 E4 E4 D4 D4 C4".split()
rhythm = [quarter] * 6 + [half] + [quarter] * 6 + [half]
melody = [
    omk.NoteEvent(tones={wsmn.TonalVector.from_string(p)}, duration=d)
    for p, d in zip(pitches, rhythm, strict=True)
]
clef = omk.ClefEvent(clef=treble_clef)
graph.add_line([clef, *melody])
graph.add_line_to_score(score, clef)  # the clef is the head of the line

# The harmony: its own line, pinned to the first note of the melody.
chords = [
    omk.ChordEvent(chord=C(maj), duration=whole),
    omk.ChordEvent(chord=F(maj), duration=half),
    omk.ChordEvent(chord=C(maj), duration=half),
    omk.ChordEvent(chord=F(maj), duration=half),
    omk.ChordEvent(chord=C(maj), duration=half),
    omk.ChordEvent(chord=G(dom7), duration=half),
    omk.ChordEvent(chord=C(maj), duration=half),
]
graph.add_line(chords)
graph.add_simultaneous(melody[0], chords[0])
graph.add_line_to_score(score, chords[0])

# The lyrics: a line of syllables, zipped onto the notes one syllable per onset.
verse = omk.LyricSection(section_type="verse", section_number=1)
syllables = graph.add_lyrics(
    "Twin-kle, twin-kle, lit-tle star, how I won-der what you are",
    section=verse,
)
graph.zip_lyrics_to_objects(syllables[0], melody[0])
```

Walking a line yields its events in order.
Every position is relative to some reference event;
here the reference is the first note,
and onsets are shown as fractions of a whole note.

```{python}
def lyric_on(event):
    return " ".join(
        str(s) for s in syllables
        if list(graph.edges_between(event, s, omk.EdgeType.LYRIC))
    )

print(f"{'onset':<8}{'tone':<6}{'duration':<28}lyric")
for event in graph.walk_line(melody[0]):
    onset = graph.relative_onset(melody[0], event).rational_length
    tone = next(iter(event.tones))
    print(f"{str(onset):<8}{format(tone, 'ascii'):<6}{event.duration!r:<28}{lyric_on(event)}")
```

The chord line is walked the same way,
and its onsets are still measured from the first melody note
because the two lines are pinned together.

```{python}
for event in graph.walk_line(chords[0]):
    onset = graph.relative_onset(melody[0], event).rational_length
    print(f"{str(onset):<8}{event.chord}")
```

The score names the whole:
its title, every event of every line it holds,
and the clef, which takes no time.

```{python}
print(score.title)
print(len(list(graph.walk_score(score))), "events in the score")
print(graph.relative_onset(clef, melody[0]))
```

Transposing a span of the graph transforms every tone in it.

```{python}
graph.transform_tones(melody[0], melody[-1], wsmn.TonalVector.transpose, P5)
print(" ".join(format(next(iter(e.tones)), "ascii") for e in graph.walk_line(melody[0])))
```

## A drum kit

Unpitched percussion has no pitch to name,
so a `PercussionTone` is a relative pitch and a stroke,
either or both left out:
`PercussionTone()` is a plain hit on whatever the part is,
and the ready-made ones have names.
The instrument is the `PercussionPart`,
which may carry a palette of the tones it is expected to use.
A drum kit is one part per drum, each on its own line,
held together by a `LineGroup`:
the origin its lines are measured from,
so they need no pins to be aligned.
Percussion tones have their own symbols module,
because some of their names (`heel`, `toe`) are also the names of marks.

```{python}
from openmusickit.systems.wsmn.percussion.symbols import (
    bass_drums, closed, hi_hats, hit, open_hat, snare_drums,
)


def line(*tones, duration):
    return [
        omk.Rest(duration) if tone is None else omk.NoteEvent(tones={tone}, duration=duration)
        for tone in tones
    ]


kit = omk.OmkGraph(omk.GraphMeta())
hi_hat = line(*[closed] * 7, open_hat, duration=eighth)
snare = line(None, hit, None, hit, duration=quarter)
kick = line(hit, None, hit, None, duration=quarter)
for drum in (hi_hat, snare, kick):
    kit.add_line(drum)

drums = omk.LineGroup(name="Drum kit")
kit.add_group(drums, [hi_hat[0], snare[0], kick[0]])
kit.add_stint(omk.PercussionPart(name="Hi-hat", palette=hi_hats), omk.Stint(), hi_hat[0])
kit.add_stint(omk.PercussionPart(name="Snare", palette=snare_drums), omk.Stint(), snare[0])
kit.add_stint(omk.PercussionPart(name="Kick", palette=bass_drums), omk.Stint(), kick[0])
```

Each line is walked on its own,
and onsets on any line can be measured from any event of another,
because the group relates them.

```{python}
for name, drum in (("hi-hat", hi_hat), ("snare", snare), ("kick", kick)):
    cells = []
    for event in kit.walk_line(drum[0]):
        onset = kit.relative_onset(hi_hat[0], event).rational_length
        sound = "rest" if event.is_rest else f"{next(iter(event.tones))}"
        cells.append(f"{str(onset):>4} {sound}")
    print(f"{name:<7}", "  |  ".join(cells))
```

A tone prints as its readable form,
and a remap over a line is an ordinary tone operation.

```{python}
print(f"{closed}", "/", f"{open_hat}", "/", f"{hit}")
kit.transform_tones(hi_hat[0], None, lambda tone: open_hat if tone == closed else tone)
print(" ".join(f"{next(iter(e.tones))}" for e in kit.walk_line(hi_hat[0])))
print(len(list(kit.walk_group(drums))), "events in the kit")
```
